title: Differentiating acute fatigue and overreaching during intensified training using a recursive least squares algorithm combined with the variable dose-response model
population: Eight swimmers followed for 61 weeks covering five training cycles; daily load from pool kilometres and dry-land equivalents; performance from 50-m trials twice weekly
findings: A time-varying variable dose-response model with a recursive least squares algorithm was applied; weekly changes in parameters were used to derive the modelled impulse response of a single session.
Functional overreaching appeared as a significant performance decline within four cycles of increased training, followed by a performance peak after two or three weeks of reduced training.

When increased training led to decreased performance, the modelled impulse response showed a significant increase in the acute negative effect and a decrease in the delayed positive effect of a single workout.
The authors conclude weekly variation in estimates could help diagnose overreaching and re-adjust subsequent training.
limitations: Eight swimmers, one sport, retrospective modelling of existing data; no out-of-sample test of plan adjustments. Crossref lists online 2024-12-22; Europe PMC lists the 2025 print year.
implications: Treat time-varying parameter drift as a descriptive flag for possible overreaching, never as an automatic load change.
Allow weekly re-estimation of model parameters only when performance tests are frequent (twice weekly in this study).
